name: menu
title: From a weekly menu to a shopping list
pitch: Write your recipes once. Each week, pick your meals: the program adds up the ingredients, converts the units, removes what you already have and groups the list by store aisle.

steps.do: Create the project with `cargo new menu`. Write a Recipe struct (name, servings, ingredients) and an Ingredient struct (name, quantity, unit); fill one recipe in your code and print it.
steps.hint: A recipe holds a `Vec<Ingredient>`; quantities are `f64`.
steps.why: Structs inside structs describe real data: a recipe has ingredients, each with its own fields.

steps.do: Write 3 of your real recipes in a file (TOML or JSON) and load them with serde.
steps.done: the program prints the 3 recipes from the file.
steps.hint: The toml crate reads TOML, which is pleasant to write by hand: `[[recipe]]` sections.
steps.why: Data in a file can change without recompiling. TOML is made for files people write themselves.

steps.do: Choose the week's meals from the command line: `cargo run -- pasta curry pasta`.
steps.done: the chosen recipes are printed, and an unknown name prints a clear message.
steps.hint: `.iter().find(|r| r.name == name)` returns an Option: None means not found.
steps.why: Option is how Rust says "maybe nothing". You have to handle the None case: no null pointer surprises.

steps.do: Add up the ingredients of the chosen meals in a HashMap.
steps.done: two recipes with 200 g and 300 g of rice give "rice: 500 g".
steps.why: entry() finds the key or creates it in one step. It's the Rust way to count and add up.

steps.do: Scale the quantities to the number of people: a recipe for 2, cooked for 4.
steps.hint: Multiply by people / recipe servings, as f64.
steps.why: Mixing integers and decimals needs an explicit conversion in Rust (`as f64`). Nothing changes type behind your back.

steps.do: Handle units: grams and kilograms, milliliters and liters, with an enum for the unit.
steps.done: 500 g + 1 kg gives 1.5 kg, and grams are never added to liters.
steps.hint: Convert everything to a base unit (grams, milliliters) when adding, and choose the nicest unit when printing.
steps.why: An enum makes impossible values impossible: a unit can only be one you listed. Converting to a base unit is how real software (and physics) avoids mixing units.

steps.do: Group the list by store aisle (vegetables, dairy, dry goods…), from the recipe file.
steps.done: the list prints aisle by aisle.
steps.hint: An aisle for each ingredient in the file, and a BTreeMap from aisle to ingredients to keep them sorted.
steps.why: The order of a list matters to the person using it. A sorted map gives you a stable, predictable order.

steps.do: Remove what you already have: a pantry file with what's in your cupboards.
steps.done: rice you already have is not on the list, or only the part you're missing.
steps.hint: Load the pantry into a HashMap too, and subtract.
steps.why: Same data structure, used the other way: once you have a map of quantities, adding and removing are easy.

steps.do: Save the shopping list to a text file you can print or send to your phone.
steps.done: the file is easy to read in the store.
steps.hint: `write!` and `writeln!` work on files like `print!` does on the screen.
steps.why: The output is what you'll use. Making it pleasant to read is part of the job, not decoration.

steps.do: Optional: plan the week by day (lunch and dinner), or pick meals at random among the ones you didn't eat last week.
steps.done: the plan has no meal twice in a row.
steps.hint: The rand crate's `choose` picks from a list; keep last week's plan in a file.
steps.why: A small rule (no meal twice in a row) turns a random pick into a useful one.
